# 117 · Payment command sent to Kafka from inside the order transaction: the outbox dropped for a dual write

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: 1 new problem** | functional | high | refactor, behaviour change intended | [`OrderService`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-service/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/app/OrderService.java) | [B12: Boundary contracts](../../lib/README.md) |

> The developer drops the outbox from the order path: `OrderService.place` sends the `ChargePayment` command to Kafka itself, from inside the MongoDB transaction that records the order, so the payment service hears about the order at once instead of on the relay's next poll. The send is not part of the transaction. A write conflict makes `Transactions.run` retry the work, and each attempt sends a fresh command with a fresh id; a transaction that rolls back after the send has told the payment service to charge for an order that does not exist; a process that dies between the commit and the send leaves an order that waits for a payment nobody was asked for. The boundary contract places every effect with respect to transactions; the regenerated contract has `sends payments.commands` under `POST /orders` and a `!` line: a transaction that sends.

Tags: [spring-boot](../README.md#tag-spring-boot), [dual-write](../README.md#tag-dual-write), [contract-diff-review](../README.md#tag-contract-diff-review)

## The change

Replace the `Outbox` in `OrderService` with a `KafkaTemplate`, and in `place` send the encoded `ChargePayment` to `payments.commands` directly, inside the `transactions.run` block that inserts the order, instead of enqueuing it in the outbox for the relay to send. `OrderController` and the payment service are untouched: the same message reaches the same topic, sooner.

import java.util.UUID;

 * placed instead of on the relay's next poll.

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final TicketingStore store;
    private final Transactions transactions;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;
    private final OrderTransitions transitions;
    private final Clock clock;

            Transactions transactions,
            KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka,
            OrderTransitions transitions,

        this.store = store;
        this.transactions = transactions;
        this.kafka = kafka;
        this.transitions = transitions;
        this.clock = clock;
    }
    // ...
                    now,
                    now);
            store.insert(order);
            var command = new PaymentCommand.ChargePayment(
                    UUID.randomUUID(), order.id(), now, order.customerId(), order.amountCents(), paymentToken);
            kafka.send(Topics.PAYMENT_COMMANDS, order.id(), MessageCodec.encode(command));
            return new Created<>(order, true);

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`:ticketing-service:test`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

The outbox exists so that the order and the command to charge for it are one atomic write: the relay sends what the committed transaction enqueued, and nothing else. With the send inside the transaction the two are a dual write. `Transactions.run` retries the work when MongoDB reports a transient error (a write conflict with a concurrent transaction on the same seats), and the retry runs the whole block again: a second `ChargePayment`, with a new command id that the payment service's inbox has never seen, so the customer is charged twice for one order. A transaction that fails to commit after the send (the second attempt also conflicts, the connection drops) has already asked the payment service to charge for an order that was never recorded; the `PaymentCaptured` event comes back for an order the ticketing service cannot find. A process that dies after the commit and before the send, or whose send times out, leaves an order in `PENDING_PAYMENT` with no command on the topic and nothing to retry it. No test sees any of this: the system tests run with one client at a time, so no transaction conflicts, and the Kafka topic receives the command either way.

## Why the verdict is right

The reach lines of a boundary contract place each effect with respect to transactions: inside a transaction the method opens (its own `@Transactional`, or a lambda it hands to a `TransactionTemplate` or to a helper that runs its argument through one, which is what `Transactions.run` is), or with no transaction on the path. Before the change `POST /orders => ResponseEntity<Order> place(@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrder request)` has `reads HoldDocument, OrderDocument, SeatDocument` and `writes OrderDocument, Outbox.Entry` under it, and no `!` line: the outbox entry is a document written in the same transaction as the order. The change is a refactoring in the developer's eyes (the command still reaches the topic), so the runner regenerates the contract and the reviewer reads the diff: the route's writes line loses `Outbox.Entry`, it gains `sends payments.commands`, and the line `! a transaction that sends to payments.commands: the send is not part of the transaction, so a rollback leaves the message sent and a crash before the send leaves the commit unannounced`. The new `!` line is the violation.

## What to do

Keep the outbox: the command is a document written in the order's transaction, and the relay sends it after the commit, as many times as it takes, under the message id the inbox on the other side deduplicates by. If the latency of the relay's poll is the complaint, shorten `boxoffice.outbox.poll-interval`, or have the relay woken by the transaction's commit (a `@TransactionalEventListener` that nudges it, which runs after the commit and sends nothing itself). A send that must be in the handler belongs after `transactions.run` returns, with the order recorded first and the command idempotent under the order id, which is a different design the contract would show as `sends payments.commands` with no `!` line. Either way the `!` line goes, and the diff under `POST /orders` is the one the reviewer approves.

## Notes

- The first example of the transaction placement of the reach lines (`lib/src/reach.rs`): the walk from each entry point carries a scope, outside any transaction, inside one the root opened, or inside a `@Transactional` method of another class, and the effects go into `all`, `outside` and `inside` sets. The root is inside its own transaction when it is `@Transactional` (with a propagation that joins or opens one); a lambda enters the root's transaction when it is an argument of a call to `TransactionTemplate.execute` or `executeWithoutResult`, or to a method (a runner) that reaches either of those or a `@Transactional` method: Box Office's `Transactions.run(Supplier)` calls `template.execute`, and `run(Runnable)` calls that, so a lambda handed to either is inside. A `@Transactional` method of another class on the path takes its effects for itself (its own member in the contract carries them), so the `!` line sits under the service method and not under every route that calls it; a `@Transactional` method of the same class is a self-invocation, which the proxy does not see, and changes nothing.
- Four checks read the placement: a send (Kafka, RabbitMQ, JMS, Spring Cloud Stream, SQS, SNS, a `MessageChannel`) inside the root's transaction is `! a transaction that sends to ...` (left alone when `spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix` is set in an application file, which makes the Kafka producer transactional and synchronises its commit with the database's: not atomic, but not the plain dual write); an HTTP call inside it is `! a transaction that calls POST /...: the call is not part of the transaction, so a rollback does not undo it, and the transaction stays open for the round trip`; an event published with no transaction on the path, when a method of the module (or a sibling) is a `@TransactionalEventListener` for that event type without `fallbackExecution = true`, is `! publishes E outside a transaction: ...`, since Spring drops the event when no transaction is active; and a `@TransactionalEventListener` whose phase is not `BEFORE_COMMIT` and whose reach writes is `! an AFTER_COMMIT listener that writes ...` unless it is `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)` or `@Async`: after the commit the transaction's resources are still bound to the thread and nothing commits again, so a JPA or JDBC write there is never committed (Spring's documentation of `TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT` says the same). The Box Office contracts regenerated unchanged: no module sends from inside `Transactions.run`, the outbox relay sends from a `@Scheduled` method with no transaction, and nothing publishes application events.
- What the placement does not know: a transaction driven by hand through a `PlatformTransactionManager`, a lambda a runner takes but runs after its commit (it is placed inside), a `@Transactional` on a Kafka or JMS transaction manager (read as a database transaction, so a send under it is still flagged), and the retry in `Transactions.run`, which is what turns this dual write into a double charge: the `!` line says the send is not part of the transaction, and the reviewer, who knows the helper retries, draws the rest. The writes line also changes in this example (`Outbox.Entry` leaves it), which a reviewer who knows what the outbox is for would stop at on its own; the `!` line is there for the one who does not.
- The change is a refactoring in the developer's eyes because the same command reaches the same topic; the page keeps it as `refactor` with the behaviour change marked intended, since the point is the shortcut's cost showing up under the route the reviewer reads. The patch changes the Java of the module, so the runner compiles it with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`. The Spring Boot tests of the module need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.
- The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): `POST /orders`: the `MongoTemplate.insert` effect is changed (the old build writes `Outbox.Entry` by it inside its transaction and the new one doesn't, with the outbox entry's payload paths gone), and beside it the comparison names what the new build attempts instead: `sends to payments.commands, inside its transaction, in OrderService.lambda$place$0`. The `KafkaTemplate.send` is a new attempt in the route's trace. Statically the comparison sees an effect replaced by another; the dual write and its retry duplicate are for the trace proof (O3) and the boundary contract's `!` line.

**Provenance:** Constructed from the dual-write problem that the transactional outbox pattern answers (a message sent inside a database transaction is neither committed nor rolled back with it), on the Box Office order path because its outbox is there for exactly this and a developer in a hurry sees it as an extra hop, and from the retry in `Transactions.run`, which makes the double send concrete.

## Reproduce

```bash
python3 examples/tools/build.py 117
```

This applies `change.patch` to a temporary copy of the repo, runs the verifier on it, and rewrites this page.
